title: Minimally invasive tubular decompression versus traditional open surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
article_subtype: Systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative studies
condition_or_topic: Minimally invasive tubular decompression versus open laminectomy for symptomatic degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS).
clinical_background: LSS involves narrowing of lumbar neural passageways and can cause pain, radiculopathy, or neurologic claudication. It affects about 11% of U.S. adults and approximately 103 million people worldwide. When conservative treatment fails, surgery may be considered. Open laminectomy decompresses neural structures but requires substantial disruption of paraspinal muscles and other tissues. Tubular decompression uses a muscle-sparing surgical corridor. Earlier comparisons were limited by small samples, inconsistent outcomes, older data, or the pooling of tubular surgery with other minimally invasive techniques, leaving uncertainty about the relative merits of these approaches.
objectives: To systematically review and meta-analyze comparative evidence on minimally invasive tubular decompression versus traditional open laminectomy in adults with symptomatic degenerative LSS.
To assess clinical outcomes, perioperative parameters, and complication rates specifically for tubular decompression rather than combining it with other minimally invasive techniques.
clinical_question: In adults with symptomatic degenerative LSS, how does minimally invasive decompression using tubular retractors compare with traditional open laminectomy for surgical parameters, perioperative and postoperative complications, patient-reported outcome measures, and hospital length of stay?
study_design: PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis of comparative observational studies. The authors searched PubMed, Ovid Embase (Elsevier), and CENTRAL for records from January 2015 to April 2025, with the final search on April 24, 2025. Eligible designs were retrospective cohort and case-control studies published in English. Trial registries, citation networks, and bibliographies were also screened, but the synthesis included only peer-reviewed comparative studies.

population.description: Adults with symptomatic degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis treated with minimally invasive tubular decompression or traditional open laminectomy. The analysis comprised 2,860 patients across ten cohorts.
inclusion_criteria: Patients aged 18 years and older with lumbar spinal stenosis.
Comparative studies of decompression using tubular retractors versus traditional open laminectomy.
Patients with associated spondylolisthesis were eligible when treated with decompression alone.
Retrospective cohort or case-control studies published in English between January 2015 and April 2025.
Studies reporting patient-reported outcomes at ≥ 3 months when contributing to those analyses.
exclusion_criteria: Cohorts treated with decompression plus fusion or revision surgery.
Animal or experimental studies, reviews, systematic reviews, non-English publications, and studies comparing other surgical procedures or combined techniques.
Publications from the same investigators or collaborative research consortium when their inclusion risked duplicating patient cohorts.

interventions: Minimally invasive decompression performed with tubular retractors.

primary: Overall surgical complications, dural tears, surgical site infections, and reoperation.
Perioperative measures including estimated blood loss, operative time, and hospital length of stay.
Patient-reported outcomes measured with ODI, VAS-B, and VAS-L.

statistical_methods: The authors pooled continuous outcomes as mean differences using metacont() and binary outcomes as odds ratios using metabin(), applying inverse-variance random-effects models in R software (v4.5.0). Change scores were calculated as follow-up minus preoperative values when both were available; their standard deviations were estimated using Corr = 0.5. When means and standard deviations were unavailable but ranges were reported, estimates used SD ≈ (max – min)/4 and mean ≈ (min + 2 × median + max)/4. I² quantified heterogeneity, with values greater than 50% considered substantial. Prespecified common-effect models assessed the sensitivity of patient-reported outcomes; leave-one-out analyses were performed for outcomes with ≥5 studies. Perioperative outcomes were also checked after excluding the discectomy cohort reported by Kumar et al. (2022).
follow_up: No minimum follow-up was required for perioperative outcomes; patient-reported outcomes required assessment at ≥ 3 months.
quality_assessment_tool: Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) for study quality and GRADE for certainty of evidence.
interpretation: Compared with open laminectomy for LSS, MI tubular decompression was associated with fewer overall complications and surgical site infections, less EBL, and shorter LOS. Reoperation rates, surgical time, ODI, and VAS-L did not differ significantly. Dural tears were less frequent with the tubular approach, but the difference was not statistically significant. VAS-B favored the tubular approach in the common-effect analysis, whereas the primary random-effects analysis found no significant difference; the authors therefore regard the possible back-pain benefit as uncertain. Several outcomes showed substantial between-study heterogeneity, warranting cautious interpretation.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The reductions in EBL and surgical site infections agree with earlier reports, although previous reviews comparing minimally invasive and open approaches have produced inconsistent findings. The authors distinguish their review by focusing specifically on tubular decompression rather than combining different minimally invasive techniques. Kumar et al. described an early learning curve with more complications and longer procedures. On dural injury, Aspalter et al. reported similar incidental durotomy rates between minimally invasive and open surgery, Boukebir et al. reported incidental durotomy in 31 of 313 microtubular cases, and Sharma et al. reported significantly fewer dural tears with a minimally invasive approach. In a different indication, Liu et al. found comparable efficacy for tubular and open microdiscectomy; Chin et al. reported possible blood-loss and hospitalization advantages with endoscopic decompression but better visualization and greater anatomical familiarity with tubular retractors.
clinical_implications: The observed reductions in blood loss, infection, complications, and hospitalization may make tubular decompression particularly relevant for older patients and patients with comorbidities.
Lower tissue disruption may reduce physiological burden and hospital resource use.
The authors consider dural integrity at least comparable between approaches, while acknowledging that their pooled dural-tear result was not statistically significant.
Comparable reoperation rates suggest that the perioperative advantages were not accompanied by a detected increase in subsequent surgery.

Preservation of musculature and posterior stabilizing structures could reduce later slip progression or the need for fusion, but the authors present this as a potential advantage rather than an established outcome.
practice_implications: Tubular-assisted decompression may be considered a preferable option when feasible and when patients and care settings are appropriately selected.
Patients whose predominant symptom is low back pain should be told clearly that the procedure primarily aims to relieve leg symptoms and improve walking capacity, not directly treat back pain.
The approach may be especially attractive for older or comorbid patients and in ambulatory pathways, provided perioperative support and surgeon experience are adequate.
The authors favor supervised training with progressively more complex cases to address the tubular approach’s learning curve.
limitations: Only nine studies comprising ten cohorts were included, limiting statistical power and generalizability; the small evidence base also reduces the ability to detect smaller clinically important differences.
Kumar et al. contributed two cohorts to several outcomes, potentially giving one source disproportionate weight and reducing the robustness of pooled estimates.
Most cohorts were retrospective, increasing susceptibility to selection bias, confounding, and inconsistent data quality.
Differences in follow-up duration impede direct comparisons, particularly for long-term outcomes; data beyond >1 year were sparse.

Substantial heterogeneity remained despite random-effects modeling for overall complications (I² = 64.4%), EBL (I² = 96.8%), LOS (I² = 91.9%), and surgical time (I² = 97.2%). The authors suggest differences in patients, techniques, surgeon expertise, and postoperative care as possible contributors.
Only four studies contributed to VAS-B. Its I² (~72%) and differences in follow-up timing and baseline pain severity limit confidence in a pooled back-pain effect and temper interpretation of PROMs.
Yolcu et al. and Mueller et al. may have had disproportionate influence on particular estimates, although omitting either study did not change the overall conclusions in the leave-one-out analyses.
Estimating means and standard deviations when explicit post-treatment values were unavailable may have introduced bias or imprecision.

All outcomes involved fewer than 10 studies, and information on unpublished studies was scarce. The authors did not perform small-study-effect tests or produce funnel plots, so publication bias cannot be excluded.
Restricting inclusion to English-language studies and not quantitatively synthesizing gray literature may have introduced language or publication bias.
strengths: The review isolated tubular decompression instead of pooling disparate minimally invasive techniques and incorporated more recent evidence on instrumentation and surgical experience.
Leave-one-out analyses indicated that the principal conclusions persisted after exclusion of influential studies.
open_questions: Whether tubular decompression provides a reproducible reduction in VAS-B remains uncertain.
Whether decompression should be accompanied by fusion in patients with Grade 1 spondylolisthesis without clear instability remains controversial.
Long-term outcomes and the best criteria for selecting patients for tubular decompression remain to be established.
future_directions: Conduct larger, more homogeneous, high-quality studies to clarify the VAS-B finding, assess long-term outcomes, and improve patient selection.
Analyze other minimally invasive methods, including endoscopic procedures, separately rather than grouping them with tubular approaches.
Standardize training pathways and report surgeon experience or volume in future studies.
Develop consistent definitions and guidelines for tubular-assisted procedures to improve communication, research comparability, and patient education.

notable_adverse_events: Overall surgical complications: MI tubular decompression versus open surgery, OR 0.42, 95% CI [0.21; 0.86], p = 0.0165; absolute event rates were not given.
Dural tears: MI tubular decompression versus open surgery, OR 0.53, 95% CI [0.28; 1.03], p = 0.0604; the difference was not statistically significant, and absolute event rates were not given.
Surgical site infections: MI tubular decompression versus open surgery, OR 0.28, 95% CI [0.11; 0.69], p = 0.0055; absolute event rates were not given.
Reoperation: MI tubular decompression versus open surgery, OR 0.88, 95% CI [0.61; 1.27], p = 0.4961; the difference was not statistically significant, and absolute event rates were not given.

secondary_results: The Results section reports 5,092 identified articles: 2578 from PubMed, 2,325 from Embase, 186 from CENTRAL, and three from additional sources. Nine studies comprising ten cohorts and 2,860 patients entered the analysis. The abstract instead states that the analysis drew on 2,853 records.

For estimated blood loss, Yolcu et al. (2021) reported an MI-versus-open MD of -130.88 mL, 95% CI [-145.93; -115.83]. After excluding that study, the pooled difference still favored MI tubular decompression: MD = −27.47 mL, 95% CI −40.76 to −14.17; p < 0.0001.

For hospital length of stay, Yolcu et al. (2021) reported an MI-versus-open MD of -1.75 days, 95% CI [-1.91; -1.59]. After excluding that study, the pooled difference still favored MI tubular decompression: MD = −1.33 days, 95% CI −2.04 to −0.63; p = 0.0002.

For overall complications, Mueller et al. (2019) reported an MI-versus-open OR of 0.09, 95% CI [0.02; 0.41]. After excluding that study, the pooled advantage for MI tubular decompression persisted: pooled OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.96; p = 0.036.

Kumar et al. (2022) supplied separate MITDS (n = 32) and MITD (n = 8) cohorts, each with its own open-surgery comparator. Only the decompression cohort contributed to LSS-specific PROMs; perioperative outcomes were also checked in sensitivity analyses excluding the discectomy cohort.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that MI tubular decompression for LSS has perioperative advantages over open laminectomy, with fewer overall complications and surgical site infections, less blood loss and shorter hospital stays. ODI and VAS-L outcomes were comparable; the VAS-B finding favored the tubular approach only in the common-effect analysis, so the authors call for higher-quality research on long-term outcomes and patient selection.
narrative_summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared MI tubular decompression with conventional open laminectomy in adults with symptomatic degenerative LSS. It synthesized nine studies comprising ten cohorts and 2,860 patients, using random-effects models as the primary analyses. Compared with open surgery, the tubular approach was associated with fewer overall complications (OR 0.42, 95% CI [0.21; 0.86], p = 0.0165) and surgical site infections (OR 0.28, 95% CI [0.11; 0.69], p = 0.0055). Estimated blood loss was lower (MD -46.65 mL, 95% CI [-80.89; -12.41], p = 0.0076), and hospital stay was shorter (MD -1.39 days, 95% CI [-1.99; -0.79], p = 0.0001). Differences in dural tears, reoperation, surgical time, ODI and VAS-L did not reach statistical significance. For VAS-B, the random-effects result was not significant (MD = -0.45, 95% CI [-1.06; 0.17], p = 0.15), whereas the common-effect sensitivity analysis favored tubular surgery (MD = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.88; -0.45], p < 0.0001). The authors describe the back-pain signal as promising but uncertain. Interpretation requires caution because most cohorts were retrospective, follow-up varied and heterogeneity was substantial for several outcomes. The authors consider tubular decompression a potentially preferable option when feasible in appropriately selected patients and settings, while emphasizing the need for stronger long-term evidence.

document_sections.heading: Highlights
document_sections.content: The authors highlight fewer overall complications and surgical site infections with MI tubular decompression than with open laminectomy. They also highlight less blood loss, shorter hospital stays, and a favorable trend in VAS-B scores.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: MI tubular decompression is intended to limit soft-tissue injury relative to open laminectomy in lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS). This PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis compared the procedures in adults with symptomatic degenerative LSS. Comparative studies published from 2015–April 2025 were sought in PubMed, Embase, and CENTRAL. Outcomes covered surgical measures, complications, patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), and hospital length of stay (LOS). Random-effects models were the primary analyses; PROMs also underwent a common-effect sensitivity analysis, and I² assessed heterogeneity. The abstract reports nine studies, ten cohorts, and 2,860 patients selected from 2,853 records. Relative to open surgery, MI tubular surgery was associated with fewer overall complications (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21–0.86), fewer surgical site infections (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.11–0.69), less estimated blood loss (MD −46.65 mL, 95% CI −80.89 to −12.41), and shorter LOS (MD −1.39 days, 95% CI −1.99 to −0.79). Reoperation, operative time, dural tears, and PROMs did not differ significantly. The authors suggest that tubular-assisted decompression may reduce perioperative morbidity and resource use while providing similar patient-reported outcomes. They urge caution because of between-study heterogeneity and the predominance of retrospective cohorts, but suggest that it may be preferable when feasible for appropriately selected patients and settings.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: LSS involves narrowing of the central canal, lateral recesses, or neural foramina and compression of lumbar neural structures; possible manifestations include pain, radiculopathy, and neurologic claudication. It affects about 11% of U.S. adults and approximately 103 million people worldwide. It is a frequent reason for spinal surgery in adults over the age of 65, as age-related degeneration contributes to the condition. Conservative care includes physiotherapy emphasizing core exercises, oral medications such as NSAIDs, and epidural steroid injections when pain persists. Failure of these measures can lead to decompression with or without fusion, depending on accompanying radiographic pathology. Open laminectomy has been the standard surgical approach: removal of all or part of the lamina, the ligamentum flavum, and, when indicated, parts of the medial facets decompresses neural structures. Although it relieves symptoms, extensive paraspinal muscle and soft-tissue dissection and retraction, together with disruption of the posterior tension band, can increase postoperative complications and prolong recovery. MI tubular microsurgical decompression, often performed as ULBD, uses sequential dilators and a tubular retractor to create a muscle-sparing corridor for targeted decompression under microscope visualization. Prior reports have associated tubular methods with symptom relief, less estimated blood loss, shorter operations, fewer reoperations and infections, earlier discharge, preservation of stability, and less muscle and soft-tissue injury. Earlier meta-analyses were constrained by small samples, inconsistent outcomes, older data, and the grouping of tubular procedures with other MI approaches, including endoscopy. Developments in tubular instruments and increasing outpatient use of MI spine surgery have broadened options, but uncertainty remains about the preferable approach for LSS. The authors therefore undertook an updated systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to tubular-based MI decompression versus conventional open laminectomy in adults with symptomatic degenerative LSS, assessing clinical outcomes, perioperative measures, and complications.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The review used publicly available sources rather than patient data. The authors state that IRB approval and informed consent were therefore unnecessary, including under the cited human-subjects regulations (45 CFR §46). They followed the Cochrane Handbook and PRISMA guidance and registered the review with PROSPERO.

document_sections.heading: Eligibility Criteria and Search Strategy
document_sections.content: Using PICOs, the authors specified patients aged 18 years and older with LSS, MI decompression using tubular retractors, and traditional open laminectomy as the comparator. Outcomes included surgical parameters, perioperative and postoperative complications, PROMs, and LOS. Perioperative endpoints had no minimum follow-up; PROMs required assessment at ≥ 3 months. Patients with associated spondylolisthesis were eligible if treated with decompression alone. Decompression with fusion and revision-surgery cohorts were excluded. Eligible designs were English-language retrospective cohort and case-control studies. Animal and experimental studies, reviews, systematic reviews, non-English publications, and comparisons involving other techniques, fusion, combined procedures, or revisions were excluded. Trial registries and gray literature, including ClinicalTrials.gov, were checked for in-press records, but synthesis was limited to peer-reviewed comparative studies. Three authors independently searched PubMed, Ovid Embase (Elsevier), and CENTRAL for records from January 2015 to April 2025; the final search was on April 24, 2025. Database-specific strategies are in Appendix S1.

document_sections.heading: Study Selection and Data Extraction
document_sections.content: Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, then assessed potentially eligible full texts. They also examined included studies’ bibliographies, trial registries, and papers citing included articles. Publications from identical investigators or the same international research consortium were excluded to limit duplicate patient cohorts. Disagreements were referred to the senior author. Two authors independently entered data into a standardized Excel sheet and checked them against the original reports; the senior author adjudicated unresolved differences. Kumar et al. (2022) reported separate MITDS (n = 32) and MITD (n = 8) groups, each with its own open-surgery comparator. The review retained these distinct comparisons because their indications and techniques differed. Only the decompression cohort contributed LSS-specific PROMs; perioperative results were also tested after excluding the discectomy cohort. Extracted information included authors, publication year, sample size, demographics, procedures, and clinical outcomes. Table 1 summarizes the included studies’ demographic characteristics.

document_sections.heading: Risk of Bias, Quality Assessment, and Certainty of Evidence
document_sections.content: Two authors independently evaluated risk of bias, study quality, and certainty of evidence. Because the included studies were observational or retrospective cohorts, they assessed quality with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), reported in Table 2. GRADE was used for critical outcomes, considering bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and possible publication bias; Table 3 presents those assessments. They explicitly assessed bias from missing results and downgraded certainty when plausible selective reporting or other reporting bias was identified. Assessment disagreements were discussed with the senior author.

document_sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: The meta-analysis compared tubular-retractor MI decompression with conventional open laminectomy for LSS. Studies contributed numerical preoperative and postoperative PROMs, along with demographic, clinical, and complication data for each approach. Data were curated manually, and analyses used R software (v4.5.0).

document_sections.heading: Data Extraction and Processing
document_sections.content: For continuous endpoints, the authors extracted means and SDs before surgery and at follow-up. Where both measurements existed, the endpoint was the follow-up-minus-preoperative change. They approximated change-score variability using SDChange = SD21 + SD22 - (2 × Corr × SD1 × SD2), with Corr = 0.5. When reports supplied ranges rather than means and SDs, they estimated SD ≈ (max – min)/4 and mean ≈ (min + 2 × median + max)/4, assuming an approximately normal distribution. For binary endpoints, they extracted event counts and group totals.

document_sections.heading: Meta-Analytic Strategy
document_sections.content: The primary analyses used random-effects models in the R meta package. Continuous outcomes measured consistently across studies were pooled as MD with metacont(); examples included operative duration, LOS, and estimated blood loss. Binary outcomes were pooled as OR with metabin(). Both types used inverse-variance weighting to account for between-study heterogeneity. Random-effects estimates took precedence in interpretation. Because a small number of studies used identical PROM scales, prespecified common-effect models provided a sensitivity analysis under the assumption of a shared underlying effect without between-study heterogeneity. Outcomes supported by ≥5 studies also underwent leave-one-out influence analyses, whose qualitative effects were reported in Results.

document_sections.heading: Heterogeneity and Reporting
document_sections.content: The authors quantified heterogeneity with I² and considered values greater than 50% substantial. They reported pooled effects, 95% confidence intervals, p-values, and I², and displayed results in forest plots.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The search identified 5,092 articles: 2578 from PubMed, 2,325 from Embase, 186 from CENTRAL, and three from other relevant sources. Nine studies comprising ten cohorts and 2,860 patients entered the analysis. Compared with open surgery, MI tubular surgery had fewer overall complications across six studies (n = 2167): OR 0.42, 95% CI [0.21; 0.86], p = 0.0165, with I² = 64.4%, p = 0.0153. Five studies (n = 1327) suggested fewer dural tears, but not significantly: OR 0.53, 95% CI [0.28; 1.03], p = 0.0604; I² = 5.4%. Surgical site infections were significantly less frequent with MI surgery in four studies (n = 1947): OR 0.28, 95% CI [0.11; 0.69], p = 0.0055; I² = 2.9%. Reoperation did not differ significantly across seven studies (n = 2730): OR 0.88, 95% CI [0.61; 1.27], p = 0.4961; I² = 0%. Estimated blood loss was lower with MI surgery: MD -46.65 mL, 95% CI [-80.89; -12.41], p = 0.0076; I² = 96.8%, p < 0.0001. LOS was shorter: MD -1.39 days, 95% CI [-1.99; -0.79], p = 0.0001; I² = 91.9%, p < 0.0001. Operative time showed no significant difference across seven studies (n = 1457): MD 2.78 minutes, 95% CI [-16.71; 22.27]; I² = 97.2%, p < 0.0001. Yolcu et al. (2021) contributed notably to the lower blood-loss estimate (MD -130.88 mL, 95% CI [-145.93; -115.83]) and shorter LOS estimate (MD -1.75 days, 95% CI [-1.91; -1.59]). Mueller et al. (2019) reported a notably lower complication rate (OR 0.09, 95% CI [0.02; 0.41]). Excluding Yolcu et al. reduced the estimated advantages without removing significance for blood loss (MD = −27.47 mL, 95% CI −40.76 to −14.17; p < 0.0001) or LOS (MD = −1.33 days, 95% CI −2.04 to −0.63; p = 0.0002). Excluding Mueller et al. weakened but retained the overall-complication advantage (pooled OR = 0.53, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.96; p = 0.036). ODI showed no significant difference across four studies (n = 743): MD = -1.88, 95% CI [-5.92; 2.16], p = 0.36; I² = 43.0%, p = 0.1533. For VAS-B, four studies (n = 596) showed no significant difference under random effects (MD = -0.45, 95% CI [-1.06; 0.17], p = 0.15), whereas the common-effect analysis favored tubular surgery (MD = -0.66, 95% CI [-0.88; -0.45], p < 0.0001); heterogeneity was I² = 71.8%, p = 0.0138. VAS-L pain reduction did not differ significantly across four studies (n = 596): MD = 0.18, 95% CI [-0.10; 0.46], p = 0.2; I² = 37.3%, p = 0.1880.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The authors interpret tubular decompression as associated with fewer overall complications and surgical site infections, less estimated blood loss, and shorter LOS than open laminectomy, while PROMs were generally comparable. Several endpoints were heterogeneous. They suggest that differences in surgeon experience, equipment, and perioperative care probably contribute to variation in blood loss, LOS, and operative time. Kumar et al. reported steep learning curves for MITDS and MITD, with more complications early in practice and shorter operations as experience increases. Reported equipment ranged from a 22 mm three-blade tubular retractor system (Globus MARS 3V) to 16–20 mm tubular retractors. Evaniew et al. described substantial institutional variation, including perioperative management. Another included report observed postoperative disc herniation more prominently after multilevel procedures, suggesting that procedural complexity may contribute to between-study variation. The lower blood loss and surgical site infection rates agree with earlier reports. The authors consider reduced tissue disruption particularly pertinent to older patients with comorbidities that can increase postoperative risk; they state that limiting blood loss and tissue trauma can help preserve immunity, prevent infection, and support healing. They see a possible VAS-B advantage, alongside similar VAS-L and ODI outcomes. Patients whose main symptom is low back pain should be told clearly that the procedure principally aims to improve leg symptoms and walking, rather than directly treat back pain. The authors describe low back pain as multifactorial, citing facet arthropathy, scoliosis, and sagittal malalignment. They present a proposed explanation—not an established effect—in which decompression reduces compensatory forward flexion, permits a more upright posture, reduces lower-back muscle strain, and might relieve back pain. They suggest that the observed benefits imply less physiological burden and hospital resource use. Dural tears trended lower with tubular surgery without a statistically significant difference, potentially reflecting the learning curve or differences in dural handling. Aspalter et al. reported similar incidental durotomy incidence with MI and open surgery; Boukebir et al. reported incidental durotomy in 31 of 313 microtubular cases; Sharma et al. found significantly fewer dural tears with an MI approach than with open surgery. The authors argue that restricting their synthesis to tubular procedures limits technique heterogeneity and that other MI techniques, including endoscopy, should be analyzed separately. In their interpretation, available studies do not consistently establish fewer durotomies with tubular decompression, but do not suggest an increased risk; they consider it at least non-inferior for dural integrity. They suggest that less surgical dead space could reduce large pseudomeningoceles after persistent cerebrospinal fluid leakage and note that instruments for primary dural repair through tubular retractors have been described. Reoperation rates were comparable; the authors interpret this as indicating that perioperative gains were not accompanied by more subsequent surgery. For Grade 1 spondylolisthesis without clear instability, they identify controversy over whether decompression should include fusion. They propose that greater disruption of muscles and the posterior tension band during open laminectomy could increase later slip progression or instability, whereas preservation of stabilizing structures with MI surgery might lessen progression and subsequent fusion. Earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses produced inconsistent comparisons of MI tubular and open approaches. The authors argue that their restriction to contemporary tubular decompression avoids combining dissimilar MI techniques. In lumbar disc herniation, Liu et al. found tubular microdiscectomy and open microdiscectomy similarly effective within an analysis also considering transforaminal endoscopic discectomy; the authors note that this is a different indication but illustrates the value of technique-specific comparisons. Chin et al. suggested that endoscopy may reduce blood loss and hospitalization, whereas tubular retractors offer surgeons greater visualization and anatomical familiarity. The authors state that supervised training and progressively complex cases can address the tubular technique’s learning curve. They suggest that early experience might explain longer procedures and greater variability in blood loss and LOS than at high-volume centers. They call for standardized training pathways, reporting of surgeon experience and volume, and clearer definitions and guidance for tubular-assisted procedures, including mTLIF and far lateral microdiscectomies. They argue that standards could improve communication, research consistency, patient education, and differentiation between techniques. Clinically, they consider tubular decompression potentially attractive for older or comorbid patients and for ambulatory care when perioperative support and surgeon experience are adequate.

document_sections.heading: Limitations
document_sections.content: Only nine studies and ten cohorts were included, restricting statistical power and generalizability. For outcomes including ODI, VAS-L, VAS-B, operative time, LOS, and estimated blood loss, Kumar et al. supplied two separate cohorts; this could give a single source disproportionate influence and introduce bias. Most studies were retrospective, increasing the potential for selection bias, confounding, and inconsistent data quality. Differences in follow-up hinder direct comparison, particularly for long-term outcomes. The small evidence base reduces the ability to detect smaller clinically meaningful differences, as illustrated by the near-significant dural-tear finding. Substantial heterogeneity remained despite random-effects modeling: overall complications I² = 64.4%, estimated blood loss I² = 96.8%, LOS I² = 91.9%, and operative time I² = 97.2%. The authors suggest differences in patient populations, techniques, surgeon expertise, and postoperative care as possible causes. Only four studies informed VAS-B; although I² may be imprecise with so few studies, the reported I² (~72%) indicates substantial inconsistency. The authors therefore regard the possible VAS-B benefit as promising but uncertain and call for confirmation in larger, more homogeneous cohorts. Follow-up timing and baseline pain severity may also contribute to PROM heterogeneity. Yolcu et al. and Mueller et al. may exert disproportionate influence on particular estimates. Excluding either changed some effect magnitudes but did not change the overall conclusions in leave-one-out analyses. Approximating post-treatment means and SDs when they were not explicitly reported could introduce bias or imprecision. Every outcome had fewer than 10 studies, and unpublished-study information was scarce; the authors consequently did not perform potentially underpowered small-study-effect tests such as Egger’s test or create funnel plots. Publication bias cannot be excluded. Restriction to English-language studies and the absence of quantitative gray-literature synthesis could introduce language or publication bias. Long-term (>1 year) data were sparse.

document_sections.heading: Conclusions
document_sections.content: For LSS, the authors conclude that MI tubular decompression has perioperative advantages over conventional open laminectomy: fewer overall complications and surgical site infections, less estimated blood loss, and shorter LOS. ODI and VAS-L outcomes were comparable. VAS-B did not differ significantly under random effects, although the common-effect model indicated a statistically significant reduction favoring MI surgery; the authors describe this as a favorable trend. They regard tubular decompression as a safe, beneficial option and call for further high-quality studies of long-term outcomes and patient selection.
